Abstract: Large language models are vulnerable to jailbreak and prompt injection attacks, and most existing defenses rely on a single, human-crafted global system prompt. This paper proposes a method that automatically optimizes only the suffix of the system prompt on a per-cluster basis while keeping the model parameters and the global prefix fixed. We cluster attack prompts using k-means on the model's final hidden states, and, for each cluster, learn a suffix through an Analyzer-Rebuilder loop. Author Affiliations: Faculty of Secure IT, ITMO University, St. Petersburg, Russia; Faculty of Secure IT, ITMO University, St. Petersburg, Russia; Laboratory of Computer Security Problems, St. Petersburg Federal Research Center of the Russian Academy of Sciences (SPC RAS), St. Petersburg, Russia
Publication Title: 2026 International Russian Automation Conference (RusAutoCon)
Abstract: Distributed large language model infrastructures create fundamentally new semantic attack surfaces involving orchestration layers, retrieval pipelines, autonomous agents, moderation systems, distributed memory components, and adaptive guardrails. Existing adversarial testing methods are inadequate for enterprise-scale semantic ecosystems. The combinatorial explosion renders manual prompt engineering unscalable, and stochastic moderation causes static optimization techniques to degrade rapidly. This paper presents a cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning framework for controlled competitive testing of distributed LLM systems modeled as a decentralized partially observable Markov decision process (Dec-POMDP). Two agents jointly select semantic strategy classes and representation-layer transformations in a coordinated ten by ten action space. The study evaluates Value-Decomposition Networks (VDN) and QMIX against Independent Q-learning and random exploration. The experiment was run for 300,000 epochs per algorithm with probabilistic blocking, replay-buffer training, target networks, and a fixed random seed. The results show that value factorization stabilizes cooperative search under partial observability: QMIX and VDN achieve close asymptotic performance and outperform Independent Q-learning and the random baseline. The framework is positioned as a defensive, auditable testing method with explicit reward formalization, governance constraints, and reproducibility requirements.

Abstract: Deploying large language model (LLM)-based information retrieval systems in any organizational setting introduces critical challenges in security, access control, and providing factual information. Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) now call tools and APIs in enterprise systems, creating concrete risks: hallucinated parameters, cross-tenant data leakage, and prompt injection. This paper presents an orchestration architecture for multi-tenant deployments where the LLM proposes actions and a deterministic control plane validates and executes them, organized as three hard enforcement gates (authentication and tenant resolution, role-based tool authorization, and schema validation), four advisory filters (input sanitization, retrieval scoping, execution monitoring, output compliance), and append-only audit logging. Authors: A. Segireddy

Abstract: There is a growing use of large language models LLMs in security-related workflows. There is a gap in existing benchmarks for assessing dual-use capabilities of LLMs under safety constraints. We introduce a new, unified benchmark called CybLLM, which encompasses both offensive tasks (e.g., phishing generation, exploit request) and defensive tasks (e.g., secure coding, malware, and triage with built-in safety alignment metrics. Our framework integrates offense, Defense, and utility assessments using a composite CybScore metric that balances attack refusal quality, defensive task accuracy, and safety compliance. We include more than 1000 curated prompts that span a wide range of cybersecurity domains and filter them through both ethical and governance reviews. We tested six to ten leading models such as GPT-4/5, Claude, Gemini, LLaMA, etc. using standard conditions to compare zero-shot, few-shot, and toolaugmented settings. Our research finds an essential tradeoff in terms of utility and enforcement of refusal policies; models that are strictly enforced to limit dangerous output are less able to complete beneficial tasks, while those models that have looser guardrails to increase their ability to produce utility will be less compliant with safety constraints and therefore create unsafe outputs. We also report robustness to prompt variations and hallucination rates, and find that slight changes in input prompts can decrease accuracy by 5 percent. Additionally, we observe that the best models continue to produce unsupported information when attempting to explain security-related topics. For clarity, all of our data, evaluation code, and model output are made available for transparency purposes. A public leaderboard is also established to monitor progress. No harmful exploit content is generated for offensive tasks in Cyb-LLM; instead, offensive tasks are scored based on safe refusal and constructive guidance. The Benchmark, code, and a live evaluation platform are available open source.

Abstract: Machine learning (ML) has become a default substrate for contemporary cybersecurity—from network intrusion detection and malware classification to phishing defense and security analytics over cloud telemetry. At the same time, cybersecurity is now a first-class stress test for ML: adversaries actively manipulate inputs, labels, data pipelines, and even model supply chains. Recent trends amplify both promise and risk: transformer backbones that learn directly from raw traffic or byte streams; self-supervised pretraining over petabyte-scale logs; federated and privacy-preserving learning at the network edge; and agentic large language model (LLM) copilots that triage incidents and generate remediation steps. Abstract: Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) systems have enhanced the performance of Large Language Models (LLMs) by effectively addressing challenges such as hallucinations and generating irrelevant responses. However, integrating the RAG technique into LLMs introduces privacy risks and potential data leakage issues from the retrieval pipeline. Indirect Prompt Injections (IPIs) occur when hidden instructions inside retrieved documents slip into a model’s context as trusted evidence, exploiting weak guardrails in RAG systems and leading to unauthorized data leaks, ambiguous outcomes, and policy overrides. Existing defenses rely on brittle delimiter heuristics or limited retriever adjustments, leaving RAG systems vulnerable to adversarial directives blended seamlessly into retrieved content.In this paper, we present RIPE-II, a corpus-level benchmark that evaluates IPIs under a realistic content-poisoning threat model. RIPE-II constructs delimiter-free, position-aware poisoned corpora across multiple domains and includes both textual and visual injections. Our design explicitly models mid-document placement, chunking, truncation, and cross-component propagation, reflecting how enterprise RAG systems ingest and process content. We introduce a two-stage evaluation framework that separates retrieval exposure from generation-time compliance and distinguishes embedding-based similarity from semantic override using a calibrated LLM-based judge. Across biomedical, financial, scientific, open-domain question answering, including multi-hop reasoning and web passage retrieval settings, we find that poisoned documents can reach the final model context in up to 97% of queries and rank first in up to 94% of cases, showing that retriever and reranker choices substantially shape RAG security exposure. We further show that cosine-based attack scoring can underreport semantic compromise by more than 5×, demonstrating that lexical or embedding similarity alone is insufficient for evaluating indirect prompt injection risk.

Abstract: This paper is a systematic review of the current situation regarding jailbreaking attacks and defensive against Large Language Models (LLMs). The LLMs have performed very well in the field of software engineering and conversational systems. Nevertheless, regardless of such impressive capabilities, there are general weak points, namely, to prompt injection and jailbreaking attacks. Jailbreaking is the tactically designed control of input prompts to evade safety guardrails to cause adversarial or prohibited outputs. The current paper is proposing a comprehensive taxonomy that splits attacks into target visibility: White-Box, attack seeks the exploitation of inner architecture on the basis of gradient or logit exposure, and Black-Box, where the mechanisms of attack are grounded in prompt engineering and linguistic obfuscation. This proceeds on the background of emphasizing an everlasting adversarial arms race enabled by the current trade-off between robustly helpful and ultra-safe standards of the LLM and further underscoring the ultimate significance of defenses that are robustly anti-out-of-distribution (OOD) attack vectors.

Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) such as ChatGPT, Claude, and LLaMA are rapidly transforming domains including healthcare, education, law, and finance. However, their increasing adoption in high-stakes applications raises serious safety concerns. Without sufficient safeguards, LLM-powered AI systems are vulnerable to threats such as prompt injection, training data poisoning, model theft, denial-of-service through prompt abuse, misinformation generation, adversarial examples, model inversion, data leakage, and insider misuse. These vulnerabilities can produce harmful, biased, or misleading outputs, compromise privacy, and undermine trust. To address these risks, researchers have proposed safety approaches that aim to constrain and guide model behaviour, proactively detect and resist attacks, and incorporate ethical alignment into model design. Together, these methods form a multi-layered defence that combines preventive, detective, and corrective measures to improve LLM robustness and trustworthiness. This paper presents a comprehensive review of key safety mechanisms for LLMs, categorizing them into guardrails, red teaming, adversarial training, alignment techniques, jailbreak detection and prevention, watermarking, and fuzzing. For each category, recent advances are summarized, strengths and limitations are assessed, and open challenges are identified to support safer and more reliable real-world deployment of LLMs.
